p.src: Now Cao Cao, having seen the edict hidden in the girdle, consulted with his advisers. He wished to depose Emperor Xian and choose another man of virtue to place upon the throne. Cheng Yu remonstrated: “My lord has been able to make his might resound throughout the four quarters and issue commands to all the realm only because you uphold the name of the House of Han. The lords have not yet been pacified. If you abruptly depose one sovereign and enthrone another, it will surely provoke war.” Cao Cao therefore abandoned the idea. He merely had Dong Cheng and the other four men, together with every member of their families, escorted to the several city gates and beheaded. In all, more than seven hundred people died. None among the officials and common people of the city who witnessed it could refrain from tears. A later poet lamented Dong Cheng in these verses:

p.src: Now after Cao Cao had killed Dong Cheng and the others, his anger remained unabated. Sword in hand, he entered the palace to murder Consort Dong. The consort was Dong Cheng’s younger sister. She was favored by the Emperor and was five months pregnant. That day the Emperor was in the inner palace, privately discussing Dong Cheng’s affair with Empress Fu, for as yet no word of it had reached them. Suddenly Cao Cao entered the palace wearing his sword, anger upon his face. The Emperor turned pale with alarm. Cao Cao said, “Dong Cheng plotted rebellion. Did Your Majesty know of it?” The Emperor replied, “Dong Zhuo has already been put to death.” Cao Cao shouted, “I do not mean Dong Zhuo! I mean Dong Cheng!” Trembling, the Emperor said, “We truly knew nothing of it.” Cao Cao said, “Have you forgotten cutting your finger to write the edict?” The Emperor could not answer. Cao Cao ordered the guards to seize Consort Dong and bring her before him. The Emperor pleaded, “Consort Dong is five months with child. I beg the Chancellor to show her mercy.” Cao Cao said, “Had Heaven not brought their scheme to ruin, I would already have been slain. How could I allow this woman to live and become a future menace to me?” Empress Fu pleaded, “Confine her in the cold palace. It will not be too late to kill her after she has given birth.” Cao Cao said, “Would you preserve this traitor’s spawn so it may avenge its mother?” Weeping, Consort Dong begged, “Grant me death with my body intact, and do not expose me publicly.” Cao Cao ordered a length of white silk to be brought before him. The Emperor wept and said to the consort, “When you are beneath the Nine Springs, do not bear Us any resentment!” When he finished speaking, his tears fell like rain. Empress Fu also wept bitterly. Cao Cao said angrily, “Do you still indulge in such womanish sentiment?” He ordered the guards to drag her out, and she was strangled beyond the palace gate. p.src: Cao Cao instructed the palace wardens: “Henceforth, if any imperial relative or member of an imperial clan enters the palace gates without my command, execute them. Those who fail to guard the gates strictly shall be held equally guilty.” He also assigned three thousand of his trusted men to serve as the Imperial Guard, placing them under Cao Hong’s command to keep watch. Cao Cao said to Cheng Yu, “Though Dong Cheng and his fellows have now been executed, Ma Teng and Liu Bei were also among the conspirators and must be eliminated.” Cheng Yu said, “Ma Teng has troops stationed in Xiliang and cannot be taken lightly. You should merely send him a letter of reassurance and commendation so as not to arouse his suspicion, then entice him to the capital and dispose of him there. Liu Bei is now in Xuzhou, with his forces deployed in mutually supporting positions. He too must not be underestimated. Moreover, Yuan Shao has massed his troops at Guandu and constantly harbors designs upon the capital, Xudu. If we march east even once, Liu Bei will assuredly seek Yuan Shao’s aid. If Yuan Shao takes advantage of our absence to attack, how could we withstand him?” Cao Cao replied, “No. Liu Bei is a hero among men. If we do not strike him now and wait until his wings are fully grown, it will be difficult to deal with him even in an emergency. Though Yuan Shao is strong, he is suspicious in all things and unable to decide. Why should he trouble us?”

p.src: While they were deliberating, Guo Jia entered from outside. Cao Cao asked him, “I wish to march east against Liu Bei, but Yuan Shao gives me cause for concern. What should I do?” Guo Jia replied, “Yuan Shao is slow by nature and full of doubts, while his advisers are jealous of one another. He need not concern you. Liu Bei has only lately reorganized his army, and his men’s loyalty is not yet secure. If the Chancellor leads an army east, one battle will settle the matter.” Cao Cao was delighted. “That accords perfectly with my own intention.” He therefore raised an army of two hundred thousand, divided it into five columns, and marched upon Xuzhou.

p.src: Scouts learned of this and carried the news into Xuzhou. Sun Qian first went to Xiapi to inform Lord Guan, then hastened to Xiaopei to inform Xuande. Xuande consulted with Sun Qian and said, “Only by seeking Yuan Shao’s aid can we escape this danger.” Xuande then wrote a letter and dispatched Sun Qian to the lands north of the Yellow River. Sun Qian first visited Tian Feng, related the whole affair, and asked him to arrange an audience. Tian Feng immediately brought Sun Qian before Yuan Shao, who was presented with the letter. They found Yuan Shao haggard, with his robes and cap in disarray. Tian Feng asked, “My lord, why do you look like this today?” Yuan Shao said, “I am about to die!” Tian Feng asked, “Why does my lord say such a thing?” Yuan Shao replied, “I have five sons, but only the youngest is entirely to my liking. Now he suffers from scabies and is at death’s door. How could I have any heart to discuss other affairs?” Tian Feng said, “Cao Cao is now marching east against Liu Xuande, leaving Xuchang undefended. If we lead a righteous army into this emptiness, we may preserve the Son of Heaven above and rescue the common people below. Such an opportunity is not easily won. I beg my lord to decide.” Yuan Shao said, “I too know this is the best course. But my mind is distracted, and I fear the outcome may be unfavorable.” Tian Feng asked, “What cause have you to be distracted?” Yuan Shao replied, “Of my five sons, this one alone was born most exceptional. If any misfortune befalls him, my own life is over.” He thus resolved not to dispatch his army and said to Sun Qian, “Return to Xuande and explain my reasons. If matters do not go as he wishes, he may come and join me. I shall then find means to help him.” Tian Feng struck the ground with his staff and cried, “At such a rare moment of difficulty, he lets an infant’s illness cost him this opportunity. Our great enterprise is lost! How bitterly regrettable!” Stamping his feet, he sighed deeply and departed.

p.src: When Sun Qian saw that Yuan Shao refused to mobilize, he had no choice but to hurry through the night back to Xiaopei, where he met Xuande and related the whole affair. Xuande was greatly alarmed. “If that is so, what are we to do?” Zhang Fei said, “Do not worry, elder brother. Cao Cao’s troops have come from afar and must be weary. As soon as they arrive, we should take advantage of the moment and raid their camp. Thus we can defeat Cao Cao.” Xuande said, “I had always thought you merely a brave warrior, but when you captured Liu Dai before, you showed considerable skill in strategy. The plan you offer today is also sound military strategy.” He therefore followed Zhang Fei’s advice and divided his forces to raid the enemy camp.

p.src: Meanwhile, Cao Cao was leading his army toward Xiaopei. As they marched, a violent wind suddenly arose. With a sharp crack, it snapped one of the command flags. Cao Cao ordered the troops to halt for the moment, gathered his advisers, and asked whether the omen was auspicious or ill. Xun Yu asked, “From which direction did the wind come? And what color was the flag that it broke?” Cao Cao replied, “The wind came from the southeast and snapped the command flag at the corner. The flag was blue and red.” Xun Yu said, “It signifies nothing else: Liu Bei will surely come to raid our camp tonight.” Cao Cao nodded. Suddenly Mao Jie came in and said, “A southeast wind arose just now and snapped a blue-and-red command flag. What good or evil does my lord believe it portends?” Cao Cao asked, “What is your opinion?” Mao Jie replied, “In my humble opinion, it surely signifies that someone will come to raid our camp tonight.” A later poet lamented in these verses:

p.src: Cao Cao said, “Heaven has given me warning. We must prepare against it at once.” He divided his troops into nine companies, leaving only one to pitch a decoy camp in front while the remaining eight lay in ambush on every side. That night the moon shone faintly. Xuande took the left and Zhang Fei the right, advancing in two separate forces, while only Sun Qian remained to defend Xiaopei.

p.src: Now Zhang Fei, believing his plan had succeeded, led his light cavalry ahead and burst into Cao Cao’s camp. But he saw only a few scattered men and horses; fires suddenly flared on every side, and battle cries rose in unison. Realizing he had fallen into a trap, Zhang Fei hastened out of the camp. From due east came Zhang Liao, from due west Xu Chu, from due south Yu Jin, and from due north Li Dian; from the southeast came Xu Huang, from the southwest Yue Jin, from the northeast Xiahou Dun, and from the northwest Xiahou Yuan—the troops from all eight directions closed in to attack. Zhang Fei charged left and right, parrying attacks from front and rear. But the soldiers under him had originally served in Cao Cao’s army, and when they saw how desperate matters had become, every one of them went over and surrendered. As Zhang Fei fought on, he encountered Xu Huang and battled him fiercely; then Yue Jin came racing up from behind. Zhang Fei hacked a bloody path through the encirclement and escaped, with only several dozen horsemen still following him. He wished to return to Xiaopei, but the road had already been cut off; he thought of seeking refuge in Xuzhou or Xiapi, but feared Cao Cao’s troops would intercept him. After pondering in vain for some way out, he had no choice but to head toward Mount Mangdang.

p.src: Meanwhile, Xuande led his troops in a raid on the camp. Just as they neared its gate, tremendous battle cries erupted, and a force charged out behind them, cutting off half his men. Xiahou Dun arrived as well. Xuande broke through the encirclement and fled, only for Xiahou Yuan to pursue him from behind. When Xuande looked back, he saw that only a little over thirty horsemen followed him; he hastened toward Xiaopei, but from afar saw flames rising within the city. Forced to abandon Xiaopei, he meant to seek refuge in Xuzhou or Xiapi; but again he saw Cao Cao’s forces covering the hills and filling the fields, blocking his way. Xuande thought to himself that he had nowhere to go. Then he recalled: “Yuan Shao once said, ‘If affairs do not go as you wish, you may come and join me.’ I had better seek shelter with him for the time being and devise some better plan thereafter.” He therefore rode toward the road to Qingzhou, but there encountered Li Dian blocking his path. Xuande fled north alone on horseback across the wilderness, while Li Dian captured and carried off his remaining riders.

p.src: Now Xuande rode alone toward Qingzhou, covering three hundred li a day, until he reached the foot of Qingzhou’s walls and called for the gate to be opened. The gate official asked his name and went to report to the Inspector. The Inspector was Yuan Shao’s eldest son, Yuan Tan. Yuan Tan had always respected Xuande. On learning that he had arrived alone on horseback, he immediately opened the gate to welcome him, received him in the government offices, and questioned him closely about what had happened. Xuande gave a full account of his defeat and explained that he had come to seek refuge. Yuan Tan lodged Xuande at the posthouse and sent a letter to inform his father, Yuan Shao; at the same time, he dispatched troops from his province to escort Xuande. When they reached the border of Pingyuan, Yuan Shao personally led his followers thirty li out from Ye Commandery to welcome Xuande. Xuande bowed in thanks, and Yuan Shao quickly returned the courtesy, saying, “Yesterday, because my young son was ill, I failed to send aid, and the thought has left me deeply troubled and uneasy. Now that I am fortunate enough to meet you, the longing I have cherished all my life is greatly consoled.” Xuande said, “I, the destitute Liu Bei, have long wished to place myself under your protection, but the opportunity never arose. Now Cao Cao has attacked me, and my wife and children have all fallen into his hands. Knowing that you, General, receive worthy men from every quarter, I have cast aside my shame and come directly to seek refuge with you. I beg you to take me into your service; I swear that I shall find a way to repay your kindness.” Yuan Shao was overjoyed and treated him with great generosity, and the two resided together in Jizhou.

p.src: Meanwhile, Cao Cao captured Xiaopei that very night and immediately advanced his army against Xuzhou. Mi Zhu and Jian Yong were unable to hold the city and had no choice but to abandon it and flee. Chen Deng surrendered Xuzhou. Cao Cao’s great army entered the city. Once he had settled the populace, he summoned his advisers to discuss how to take Xiapi. Xun Yu said, “Yunchang is protecting Xuande’s wife and children and will defend that city to the death. Unless we take it swiftly, I fear Yuan Shao will seize it.” Cao Cao said, “I have long admired Yunchang’s martial skill and abilities, and I wish to win him for my own service. It would be best to send someone to persuade him to surrender.” Guo Jia said, “Yunchang’s devotion to honor and loyalty runs deep; he will certainly refuse to surrender. If we send someone to persuade him, I fear he may kill the envoy.” A man stepped out from below the command tent and said, “I once made Lord Guan’s acquaintance. I am willing to go and persuade him.” They all looked and saw that it was Zhang Liao. Cheng Yu said, “Although Wenyuan is an old acquaintance of Yunchang’s, in my judgment this is not a man who can be persuaded by words alone. I have a plan that will leave him no path either forward or back. Then, if Wenyuan speaks to him, he will surely submit to you, Chancellor.” And so it is said:
